epistemicBoundary.purpose: track social, cultural, historical and institutional evidence relevant to PlayPractice, GameCategory, RuleAuthority and PlayFrame
doesNotProve: one universal cross-cultural lexical definition of game
that observed cross-cultural correlations are causal
that solitary or animal play implies reportable human-like phenomenology
that institutional recognition creates all game mechanics

evidence.source: Leisterer-Peoples et al. 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Communications DOI 10.1057/s41599-021-00785-y
evidence.sample: 907 historical/ethnographic games from Austronesian-speaking cultural groups; filtered phylogenetic subset reported for goal-structure analysis
observations: rule-based games show cross-cultural variation in goal interdependence
competitive games are common but cooperative, team-cooperative and solitary goal structures also occur
the authors explicitly created the dataset partly because older competitive definitions excluded noncompetitive game forms
same or related game descriptions can differ in rule sets across cultural groups/sources
supports: Competition != universal Game requirement
GameForm/goal topology is culturally variable
cross-cultural Game science needs raw historical/practice evidence rather than one Western category template
limits: Austronesian family is broad but not all human cultures
dataset description/coding does not by itself identify causal cultural mechanisms
historical ethnographic records vary in completeness

evidence.sample: Six Cultures observational material, children aged 3-10
observations: creative-constructive, fantasy, role play and games-with-rules varied across the six communities
cultural norms and opportunity structures were associated with which forms of play were available/encouraged
adult work expectations, freedom for exploration and access to models/materials were relevant contextual factors
supports: PlayBehavior/Practice is culturally patterned rather than one context-free developmental output
Play and Work are not stable opposites across developmental ecologies
limits: reanalysis of 1950s material
six-community sample cannot establish universal cultural laws
association/contextual interpretation is not clean intervention causality

evidence.source: Ember & Cunnar 2015 Childhood in the Past DOI 10.1179/1758571615Z.00000000031
evidence.sample: representative cross-cultural samples using eHRAF/Probability Sample Files/SCCS material
observations: children's play and work were analyzed together rather than as mutually exclusive universal domains
play objects/context and work contributions vary with local ecology/subsistence/social organization
children's activities often track adult task environments
supports: social ecology helps shape PlayPractice
Play-vs-Work classification cannot be assumed cross-culturally identical to modern Western institutional categories
limits: ethnographic coding inherits source/reporting variation
the study is not primarily a lexical category study

evidence.source: Buchholz 2019 Journal of Literacy Research DOI 10.1177/1086296X18821144
evidence.sample: 4-year longitudinal ethnography of a multi-age playground community and a game with nearly decade-long local history
observations: the game was historically maintained through embodied/oral transmission before its first official rulebook
introducing a written rulebook produced disputes over ownership, authorship and authority
written rules did not replace oral transmission and instead generated further negotiation/talk/writing
supports: CentralDesigner != necessary for stable GamePractice
Codification != automatic authority capture
rule transmission, authorship and legitimacy are constitutive social processes
GameIdentity can persist through negotiated rule variation and changing media of transmission
limits: single local community/game
ethnographic causal inference is bounded

evidence.source: Marsh 1995 Research Studies in Music Education DOI 10.1177/1321103X9500400102
observations: children varied and transmitted singing-game text, music and movement
innovation/composition was context-sensitive and social
group interaction participated in preserving and transforming game/play forms
supports: PlayPractice can be a cultural transmission process with endogenous mutation
transmission fidelity need not mean exact rule/content copying
limits: singing-game domain is not all games
does not isolate one transmission mechanism experimentally

evidence.source: Vamplew 2007 International Journal of the History of Sport DOI 10.1080/09523360701311745
evidence.sample: historical analysis of sport regulation/rule development
observations: constitutive, auxiliary and regulatory rules have distinct governance roles
gambling, fair-play ideology, economic pressures, technology and law affected rule development
modern sport rules are historically produced rather than timeless mechanics
supports: Institutional RuleAuthority is causally responsive to external social/economic/legal conditions
RuleTopology has governance/history in addition to mechanics
Game/Sport identity can be maintained through rule change rather than exact-rule permanence
limits: broad historical synthesis rather than controlled causal experiment
sport-focused

evidence.sample: comparative early institutionalization of traditional sports and e-sports
observations: institutionalization includes organizations, competitions, standardization and cultural output
traditional sport and e-sport show comparable but nonidentical institutional trajectories
supports: SportCategory can be produced/stabilized through institutional processes over an underlying game practice
institutionalization is a transformation of governance/legitimacy/practice, not proof of a new mechanical essence
limits: paper adopts a particular sport definition for analysis
comparative history cannot establish universal transition sequence

evidence.source: Howes et al. 1989 Early Childhood Research Quarterly DOI 10.1016/0885-2006(89)90015-X
evidence.sample: 62 preschool children observed during free play in three day-care centers
observations: social pretend play involved both negotiation about roles/object properties/actions and enactment of pretend episodes
negotiation and enactment were positively correlated
enactment predicted peer acceptance independently of negotiation in the reported analyses
supports: social PlayFrame can be actively negotiated and enacted
frame maintenance is not reducible to an explicit rulebook
limits: social pretend only
correlational observations cannot establish all frame mechanisms

evidence.source: Bornstein et al. 1996 Child Development DOI 10.1111/j.1467-8624.1996.tb01895.x; Smith-Nielsen et al. 2024 Infant and Child Development / PubMed 38295066
evidence.sample: naturalistic solitary and collaborative pretense in toddlers; later study of solitary pretend play in 99 four-year-old children
observations: pretend play can be observed without an active co-player
solitary pretend play exhibits symbolic/representational organization without contemporaneous social negotiation
supports: SocialNegotiation != necessary condition for PlayFrame/pretend organization
FrameAuthority can be participant-internal/self-maintained at episode time
limits: prior social learning/cultural acquisition still matters and is not removed by solitary test context
solitary pretense does not prove a wholly private origin of frame semantics

evidence.sample: 90 students assigned to control, competitive discussion game, or game-artifact/framing condition without full mechanics
observations: game vernacular/artifact framing alone produced substantial psychological effects relative to control
interest/enjoyment was higher in both game conditions, while not all intrinsic-motivation dimensions changed
supports: GameCategory/Frame cues can causally affect participant interpretation/experience even without corresponding deep mechanical change
CategoryRecognition is not merely an epiphenomenal post-hoc label
limits: framing manipulation used artifacts/vernacular, not a pure one-word category label
psychological framing effect does not mean category cue creates GameStructure

evidence.source: Eriksson et al. 2014 Judgment and Decision Making DOI 10.1017/S1930297500006756
evidence.sample: multiple online studies, almost 1,200 unique US participants across hypothetical/incentivized public-goods decisions
observations: meaningful labels such as Teamwork Game versus Paying Taxes Game influenced/selected frames and contributions
spontaneous associations and imposed labels could produce comparable frame-selection effects
supports: labels/category cues can alter expectations and policy over unchanged payoff structure
social/cultural interpretation is causally relevant to enacted behavior
limits: economic-game framing is not ordinary PlayCategory research
label effects depend on available cultural associations

observations: reported replication found strategy games associated with social complexity
reported chance/physical-skill game associations also persisted
supports: game repertoires can covary systematically with wider social organization
GamePractice is not independent from culture/social ecology
limits: correlation does not establish whether games reflect, train, cause or coevolve with social structures
older game-type taxonomy overweights competitive/winner-defined forms
